models.collectorNote: The Sport Quattro is the seven-figure summit. For the standard car, rally provenance and an unmodified drivetrain matter — many were driven as hard as the badge promised.

generations.name: Quattro (10-valve)
generations.note: Box arches and a 200 hp turbo five in European trim. In rallying, Hannu Mikkola and Michèle Mouton made four-wheel drive look inevitable.

generations.name: Sport Quattro
generations.note: The short-wheelbase Group B homologation special — 24 cm cut from the wheelbase, Kevlar panels, and over 300 hp. Built in tiny numbers to go rallying, priced accordingly ever since.

generations.name: Quattro 20V
generations.note: The final evolution: a 20-valve head and 220 hp made it the fastest and most complete of the line, just as the rally era it created was ending.

models.intro: The original — Ur-Quattro in German, ur meaning ancestral. A turbocharged five-cylinder coupe with permanent all-wheel drive, launched in 1980 when that combination did not exist in a road car. It rewrote rallying, then rewrote what a fast road car was supposed to be. Every quattro-badged Audi since — the badge is lowercase for the system now — is this car's descendant.

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: The car that made Audi credible in the premium fight. The twin-turbo V6 S4 that followed is still a tuning-scene staple.

generations.name: Fourth generation
generations.note: Bigger, sharper-suited, and the generation where the A4's cabin lead was at its widest. The supercharged S4 was the thinking person's pick.

generations.name: Fifth generation
generations.note: Aluminium-heavy, mild-hybrid late in life, and extremely good at being driven a long way in bad weather. The S4 switched to a turbo V6 with 354 hp.

models.intro: Audi's 3 Series rival and the car that made its interiors the industry benchmark. The formula has been consistent for thirty years: restrained styling, a cabin a class above, and quattro all-wheel drive as the calling card.
models.name: A4

models.collectorNote: Gated-manual first-generation cars — V8 or V10 — are the collectible specification. The V10's Lamborghini-shared engine means parts exist; the manual gearbox is the scarce part of the car.

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: Launched with a 4.2 V8 and an open-gate six-speed manual you could see working. The 5.2 V10 arrived in 2009 and turned it into a genuine Lamborghini alternative.

generations.name: Second generation
generations.note: V10 only, dual-clutch only, faster in every direction. The rear-drive RWS and later RWD cars were the purists' consolation for the lost manual.

models.intro: Audi's supercar, built on Lamborghini bones and better for being the sensible one: a V8 — then a soaring naturally aspirated V10 — behind the seats, all-wheel drive, and usability no Italian rival matched. The first generation's gated manual is already legend.
models.name: R8

models.collectorNote: First-generation cars are bought on design and condition — unmodified, low-mileage 225 coupes are the ones appreciating. The Mk3 TT RS is a future classic hiding in plain sight.

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: The icon. Early cars were recalled for high-speed stability and gained a small spoiler, which purists debate and everyone else ignores. The 225 hp 1.8T and the later 3.2 VR6 were the picks.

generations.name: Second generation
generations.note: Aluminium body panels, better dynamics, and the arrival of the TT RS: a turbo five-cylinder with deliberate echoes of the Ur-Quattro.

generations.name: Third generation
generations.note: The virtual cockpit debuted here. The final TT RS made 400 hp from its five cylinders — the right engine to end on.

models.intro: A design concept that escaped the motor show almost unchanged. The first TT was Bauhaus on wheels — a perfect geometric statement with a car underneath — and the line spent 25 years getting faster, peaking with the five-cylinder TT RS.
models.name: TT
